d.title: Four metrics, and the phase each one belongs to
d.caption: The value of this table is diagnostic. "It is slow" is not actionable; **"TTFT is 3 seconds" points at the prompt and at prefill, and "TPOT is 140 ms" points at the model size and at memory bandwidth** — and those two have almost no fixes in common. Reporting a single latency number merges them and throws the diagnosis away.

d.title: Weights are a fixed cost; the KV cache is per request
d.caption: The weight arithmetic is simple — bytes per parameter times parameters — and it is the easy half. The distinction that matters operationally is the one underneath: **weights are a fixed cost, and the KV cache is a per-request cost that grows with sequence length.** A server has enough memory for the model and then a *budget* for concurrency, which is what 3.2 is about.

d.title: Arithmetic intensity, which makes the rest of the module coherent
d.caption: Arithmetic intensity is FLOPs performed per byte moved from memory, and hardware has a ratio too — peak FLOPs divided by bandwidth. Whichever side you fall on names your bottleneck. **Prefill loads the weights once and uses them against thousands of tokens, so it is compute-bound. Decode loads the same weights to process one token, so it is memory-bound** and the compute units idle. Which gives the estimate that governs everything: decode throughput ≈ model size / memory bandwidth, so a 14 GB model on 2 TB/s cannot beat about 7 ms per token however fast its arithmetic.

d.title: The cache is worth 4.94x, and the reason is that nothing changes
d.caption: At each decode step the model attends over every previous token. The query comes from the current token, but the keys and values come from *all* of them — and **the key and value for token 7 are identical at step 8 and at step 50**. Recomputing them is pure waste, and removing that waste is measured here at 4.94× on 24 tokens after a 128-token prompt. The speedup grows with length, because the waste did.

d.title: The cache size, and two published figures it contradicts
d.caption: The formula is 2 × layers × heads × head_dim × seq_len × bytes, where the leading 2 is K and V and the last term is 2 for float16. Running it on the stated example gives **2.15 GB, where the usual figure quoted is ~1 GB** — and a batch of 16 is 34.36 GB rather than the ~16 GB usually stated. Both published numbers are about half the arithmetic. The GQA claim, by contrast, is exact: 10.74 / 1.34 = **8.0×**.

d.title: The capacity question is not whether the model fits
d.caption: A server loads the model once; everything after that costs cache, and the cache grows with each request's sequence length. So capacity is **"how many requests fit alongside it"**, and the answer falls off a cliff: 115 concurrent requests at 1,024 tokens becomes **3 at 32,768**. Which is why a long-context feature is a capacity decision rather than a configuration flag, and why the 8× from GQA is 8× the concurrency.

d.title: Why the naive cache wastes 98.8% of an allocation
d.caption: A contiguous cache must be pre-allocated for the maximum sequence length a request *might* reach, so **a request that generates 50 tokens of a possible 4,096 wastes 98.8% of what it reserved**. Paged blocks allocate as needed, so the waste is at most one partial block. The row that buys the most beyond that is sharing: uniform blocks can be shared between requests, which is what makes a common prompt prefix free rather than duplicated per request.

d.title: MQA and GQA change how much cache there is to manage
d.caption: Sections 03 and 04 are about managing the cache; this is about shrinking it, by having several query heads share one key-value head. MQA divides the cache by the head count — **64× on a 64-head model** — at some quality cost. GQA divides by heads/groups and is the compromise that won: near-MHA quality at close to MQA's size, which is why essentially every recent large model uses it. And an 8× smaller cache is 8× the concurrency from §03's table.

d.title: Quantization is a decode optimisation, and only a decode optimisation
d.caption: From 3.1: decode throughput is bounded by model size / memory bandwidth, because every token requires loading every weight. **Halving the bytes per weight halves the bytes loaded, which halves that bound** — and nothing about the arithmetic changes, because the arithmetic was never the constraint. Prefill benefits far less: it is already compute-bound and amortises one weight load across hundreds of tokens, so the dequantisation work can cost more than it saves. So quantization helps throughput and TPOT and does almost nothing for TTFT.

d.title: Six methods, and the insight worth carrying
d.caption: **AWQ's idea is the one to remember.** Not all weights matter equally: a small fraction correspond to large activations and dominate the output, and protecting those channels — scaling them before quantizing — costs almost nothing in size while recovering most of the quality uniform quantization loses. That is why AWQ generally beats GPTQ at the same bit width, and why "4-bit" is not one thing.

d.title: The one-line quantization, and what it did
d.caption: PyTorch's dynamic quantization needs no calibration data and is the first thing anyone tries. On GPT-2 it delivers the promised speedup — 1.69× — and takes perplexity from **2.0707 to 1136.9664**, a factor of 549. The model is not degraded; it is destroyed, and it will still return fluent-looking text. Which is the argument for the check: perplexity on held-out text from your own domain is cheap and catches catastrophes like this one, and a task metric from 2.12's set catches the subtler degradation perplexity misses.

d.title: Which method, decided by where it will run
d.caption: The method follows the hardware rather than a quality ranking. Note the fourth row, which is the honest option people skip past: **BF16 — no quantization at all — when the memory is there.** And the last row is a warning rather than a recommendation: 2-bit is usually treated as about 40% of the original quality, which is rarely the right trade for the memory it returns.
